intros.market: The public certificate market remains concentrated among five providers who collectively control 91.75% of issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 37.5% and Google Trust Services at 21.0%. The market HHI of 2278 indicates high concentration, though 89 trusted CAs operate across the WebPKI. A long tail of 75 smaller CAs holds full trust store inclusion despite minimal issuance volume, creating a trust surface that far exceeds operational necessity.
intros.trust: 335 root certificates are distributed across four major trust stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four stores simultaneously. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating significant operational complexity where certificate chains may validate in one browser but fail in another. Just 38 CA owners appear in all four stores, revealing substantial disagreement about which organizations merit universal trust despite the coordinated governance efforts visible in other metrics.
intros.conc: The CR3 concentration of 74.66% means three providers control nearly three-quarters of all publicly trusted certificates, creating systemic dependency on Internet Security Research Group, Google Trust Services, and DigiCert. An HHI of 2278 places the market in high concentration territory where a single operational failure or distrust event could impact a substantial fraction of the encrypted web. This concentration intersects with geographic risk, as 92.16% of issuance originates from US-incorporated entities.
intros.tail: 75 CAs operate in the market tail with minimal issuance but full trust store access, each capable of issuing certificates trusted by billions of browsers. These low-volume CAs contribute to the 1570 total incidents recorded across 54 CAs, suggesting that audit and oversight resources may not scale appropriately to operational volume. The tail amplifies the total attack surface without corresponding contribution to certificate availability or market competition.
intros.geo: 92.16% of certificate issuance originates from US-incorporated CAs despite 44 European CAs and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs holding trust store positions. Europe accounts for just 7.74% of issuance while the 23 CAs based in Asia-Pacific, Americas, and Middle East/Africa combined represent 0.09% of market volume. This geographic concentration creates regulatory and operational dependency on US-based legal jurisdiction separate from the compelled access risks analyzed in the jurisdiction tab.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold positions in public trust stores but account for only 0.08% of total issuance. These entities span jurisdictions including China, Russia, and multiple European nations where state signals intelligence capabilities intersect with certificate authority operations. Government CA presence in trusted root programs creates potential compelled disclosure vectors despite negligible market share, a risk that compounds the jurisdiction concerns present in legal framework analysis.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high risk for compelled certificate disclosure or surveillance activity: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. Two additional jurisdictions, India and Turkey, present moderate risk based on legal frameworks enabling state access to cryptographic operations. These legal risk classifications intersect with the 30 government-operated CAs in the ecosystem, though high-risk jurisdiction CAs collectively represent minimal issuance share due to their concentration in the operational tail.
intros.ops: 1570 incidents have been recorded across 54 CAs, with misissuance accounting for 611 cases and governance failures contributing 504 more. CAs self-detect only 26% of their own incidents while external researchers discover 18% and automated tools find 17%, leaving root programs to identify just 4% despite their formal oversight role. Policy failures appear in 194 incidents and disclosure failures in 139, with audits catching only 8% of issues before public discovery.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture has evolved toward modern algorithms and key sizes, though legacy roots remain in trust stores to support older infrastructure. The data shows ongoing standards compliance across active issuance hierarchies with RSA 2048 and RSA 4096 dominating current roots while ECDSA P-256 and P-384 appear in newer hierarchies. These cryptographic decisions interact with the BR readiness timeline, as certificate lifetime reductions increase the operational tempo for key ceremonies and hierarchy rotation.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have removed or restricted CA trust store access, with 14 attributed to compliance operations failures and 10 following a demonstrated pattern of issues rather than isolated incidents. The posture distribution shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance and 3 of willful circumvention, with 3 more classified as demonstrated incompetence. Median runway from distrust announcement to effective removal spans 1185 days, creating extended periods where distrusted CAs continue operating under restriction while site operators migrate away.
intros.policy: 43 active TLS issuers face cascading certificate lifetime reductions under SC-081, with only 8 ready for the 47-day limit arriving in March 2029 while 5 remain at risk even for the 100-day threshold in March 2027. This operational challenge exists within a regulatory surface that has grown 121x since 2000 to 6657 total obligations, 76% of which are mandatory requirements spanning CA/B Forum BRs, four root programs, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF/NIST standards. No new ballots have passed since 2022 despite this complexity, suggesting policy ossification even as compliance demands compound.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% Chrome and 78.0% Mozilla participation in 2019 incidents to just 18.4% Chrome and 9.9% Mozilla in 2025 across 223 total bugs. Apple engages substantively in only 5.4% of incidents while Microsoft records zero oversight participation despite maintaining 142 unique roots not present in other stores. This decline occurs as Chrome has contributed substantive analysis to 293 bugs historically and Mozilla to 249, but recent engagement shows just 112 and 47 substantive interventions respectively from a corpus of 1856 total oversight bugs.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 contribute actively, leaving 35 with zero ballot participation or meaningful engagement. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual ballot activity with 36 proposals and 1 endorsement, while Sectigo itself ranks as the top organizational contributor overall. This participation inequality means a small subset of the 89 trusted CAs shapes the governance frameworks and baseline requirements that bind the entire ecosystem, including the 75 tail CAs whose operational practices generate disproportionate incident volume.
intros.audit: Audit letters show a 31% in-period detection rate, meaning auditors identified just 129 of the 414 incidents that occurred during periods their letters ostensibly covered. 38 CAs demonstrate high transparency gaps between audit assertions and Bugzilla incident history, while 4 audit letters contain qualified opinions and 59.1% of WebTrust issues and 66.4% of ETSI issues are self-reported rather than auditor-discovered. 11 CAs changed auditors in 2025 and 9 have adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5, but the surveillance gap persists with clean audit letters coexisting with substantive operational failures that surface only through external discovery mechanisms.
